title: Kunti in the stands
hook: at the princes' tournament a stranger walks into the arena and matches Arjuna, and one woman in the stands knows him
carry: the wise see one self in everyone
tomorrow: who is Karna's father? the arena wants to know.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a stranger asked for the armor, and Karna cut it from his body. Dana: giving, even when it costs.

Yesterday's scene came from further down the road; today we're back in the order of events, and Karna still wears his armor. A great arena in Hastinapura. Drona, the princes' teacher, has arranged a day for them to show the city what they've learned. The stands are packed, Kunti among the women. The cousins ride and fight and shoot, and Arjuna outshines them all, the text says, while the crowd roars. Then a sound at the gate. Someone new walks in.
screen: `A DAY TO SHOW THEIR SKILL.` → `ARJUNA OUTSHINES THEM ALL.` → `A SOUND AT THE GATE.`

segments.voice: It's Karna, tall and shining, in his armor and earrings. He barely bows to the teachers. He turns to Arjuna and says, in effect: everything you've done, I'll do. And he does, one feat after another, while the crowd stares. Duryodhana is overjoyed. Here at last is someone to match the cousin he resents, and he embraces Karna like a friend. Then Karna asks to fight Arjuna, one against one. And now the story swings up into the stands. Kunti sees the armor and the earrings, and she knows. This is her son, the boy she set on the river, about to fight another of her sons. The text says she faints. Vidura has her revived with cool water and sandal paste, and she comes to and watches, unable to say a word. Everyone else in the stands sees two rivals. One person sees two brothers, and she can't tell anyone. Hindu teaching takes that view a step further. In the Bhagavad Gita, spoken in this same epic, on the field where these two will finally meet, Krishna says the wise see with an equal eye: they see the one Self, the atman, in every being, and every being in that Self. Rivals, strangers, enemies: underneath, one Self. Many teachers read Kunti's view from the stands as a small picture of that wisdom. The crowd sees sides. The mother sees family. And the Gita says that, seen truly, everyone in that arena is.
screen: `KARNA MATCHES ARJUNA.` · `KUNTI KNOWS, AND FAINTS.` · `TWO RIVALS, OR TWO BROTHERS.` · `THE GITA: ONE SELF IN ALL.` · then, large: `THE WISE SEE ONE SELF IN EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you're up against right now: a rival at school or work, someone on the other side of an argument. Picture their face. If you pray, join your hands and bow to them in your mind, the way Hindus greet each other with namaste. If you don't, just say quietly: the same Self, there too. Notice whether the face changes.
Karna's abandonment. A stranger matches Arjuna in the arena, and in the stands, the mother who set him adrift knows him, and keeps silent.
Your line: the wise see one self in everyone. Two rivals, two brothers, one Self. Tomorrow: who is Karna's father? The arena wants to know.

original.note: Sanskrit ātman: the Self; the Gita says the wise see it in every being.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rival shows up to challenge the hero.

what a scholar hears: the listener shares Kunti's secret, so every exchange in the arena carries a meaning the fighters can't hear; the Gita (6.29) names the wider vision.

Arjuna.meaning: Pandu's third son, the archer, son of Indra

Vidura.meaning: the maid's son, wise in dharma, uncle to the cousins

atman.meaning: the Self, the same in every being

recall: the serpent people below the waters
